description: Independent participant building a data-driven and visually engaging project for the 2026 Space Apps Challenge. Combining skills in coding, data management, and design to tackle complex space and Earth science datasets. Working solo!
summary: Terra Vox is an Earth Information Jukebox that lets anyone hear how the planet changed. It turns NASA satellite imagery back into the numbers NASA’s colour scales encode, then plays those numbers as music, live in the browser. In Duet mode the oldest year of a theme plays in the left ear and the newest in the right, through the same fixed mapping, so the change is the difference you hear. Four themes use NASA GIBS records from 1993 to 2026: wildfires (MODIS), sea level (JPL MEaSUREs), nitrogen dioxide (OMI) and methane (AIRS). Side B plays four NASA Earth Information Center visualizations. Each year is an average that tracks NOAA’s independent records (methane r = 0.992, sea level r = 0.997), and a script shows pitch, loudness, density and tempo following the data on all 11 tracks. Built for blind and low-vision listeners first: keyboard, captions, speech, three languages.
details:
What it does. Terra Vox plays NASA Earth data as live music. Each year of a satellite record is read back into the real number behind NASA’s colour scale (parts per billion of methane, centimetres of sea level), and that number sets the pitch, loudness, busyness and tempo of a short melody in C minor pentatonic, so any combination still sounds like music. In Duet mode, the oldest and newest year of a theme play at the same time, one in each ear, through the identical mapping. The change is the difference you hear. A second side plays four NASA Earth Information Center visualizations frame by frame.

Who benefits. 338 million people are blind or have moderate to severe vision loss, and climate data almost always arrives as a chart. Terra Vox works by keyboard alone, with captions generated from the data, spoken descriptions, a one-ear listening mode, reduced motion, and English, Hindi and Spanish.

How we know the sound carries the data. Each year is an average of NASA GIBS maps and tracks NOAA’s independent records (methane r = 0.992, 2003-2025; sea level r = 0.997, 1993-2018). A script runs every frame through the app’s own mapping and checks that pitch, loudness, density and tempo follow the measured value (r of at least 0.82 on all 11 tracks). Limits are stated up front in the documentation.

Tools. Vanilla JavaScript, Tone.js and the Web Audio API, three.js, Vite, a Python data pipeline (NumPy, OpenCV), GitHub Pages. Lighthouse accessibility 100; axe-core with no violations. Built solo with Claude Code (AI coding assistant) for implementation; the concept, data choices, mapping design and testing are mine. The demo video’s narration is an AI-generated voice (ElevenLabs).
